hints: Focus on the diagonal relationship, if lithium behaves like magnesium, ask yourself what magnesium and its compounds actually do.
Remember that magnesium carbonate decomposes easily on heating, while most other Group 1 carbonates do not.
Check each statement to see which one matches magnesium chemistry rather than typical sodium or potassium chemistry.
walkthrough:
**Recall the diagonal relationship**

Lithium in Group 1 has a very small, highly polarising $\text{Li}^+$ ion. This makes it behave like $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ in Group 2, not like $\text{Na}^+$ or $\text{K}^+$.

So to predict lithium chemistry, copy magnesium chemistry.

**Remember key magnesium behaviour**

Magnesium burns brightly in oxygen, reacts only slowly with cold water, and its carbonate and nitrate decompose easily on heating.

$$\text{MgCO}_3 \rightarrow \text{MgO} + \text{CO}_2$$
$$2\text{Mg}(\text{NO}_3)_2 \rightarrow 2\text{MgO} + 4\text{NO}_2 + \text{O}_2$$

**Apply this to lithium**

Lithium carbonate should also decompose on gentle heating like $\text{MgCO}_3$, unlike $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$ which is thermally stable.

$$\text{Li}_2\text{CO}_3 \rightarrow \text{Li}_2\text{O} + \text{CO}_2$$
Similarly, lithium nitrate should give the oxide plus $\text{NO}_2$ and $\text{O}_2$, and lithium metal should react gently with water and burn vigorously, just like magnesium.

options.A: Incorrect. Magnesium burns very brightly and vigorously in oxygen, so lithium is also expected to burn well, not very slowly. This statement describes low reactivity, opposite to the prediction.
options.B: Correct. Magnesium carbonate decomposes easily on heating. By diagonal similarity, lithium carbonate also decomposes on a Bunsen burner to $\text{Li}_2\text{O}$ and $\text{CO}_2$, whereas other Group 1 carbonates like $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$ are stable to heat.
options.C: Incorrect. Forming $\text{LiNO}_2$ and $\text{O}_2$ is the typical Group 1 nitrate decomposition, for example $2\text{NaNO}_3 \rightarrow 2\text{NaNO}_2 + \text{O}_2$. Magnesium-like behaviour gives oxide, $\text{NO}_2$ and $\text{O}_2$: $4\text{LiNO}_3 \rightarrow 2\text{Li}_2\text{O} + 4\text{NO}_2 + \text{O}_2$.
options.D: Incorrect. Magnesium reacts only very slowly with cold water. Lithium therefore reacts gently with water, not very violently. Violent reaction with water is characteristic of sodium and potassium, not magnesium.
